guide.summary: Unit 5 connects probability to inference. A sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies from sample to sample. You need the center, spread, and shape of sampling distributions for sample proportions, sample means, and differences of each; the conditions that justify Normal approximations; the Central Limit Theorem; and the ideas of bias and variability in estimators.

sections.heading: Statistics, parameters, and estimators
sections.body: A parameter describes a population (p, μ, σ); a statistic describes a sample (p̂, x̄, s). The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of its values across all possible samples of the same size. An estimator is unbiased if the mean of its sampling distribution equals the parameter (p̂ and x̄ are unbiased; the sample maximum is biased low for the population maximum). Variability decreases as sample size increases. Think of a target: bias is aiming off-center; variability is scatter.

sections.heading: Sample proportions
sections.body: μ_p̂ = p. σ_p̂ = √(p(1 − p)/n), valid when n ≤ 10% of the population (10% condition). The shape is approximately Normal when np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10 (Large Counts). Quadrupling n halves the standard deviation. For differences of independent sample proportions: μ = p₁ − p₂ and σ = √(p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂), approximately Normal if all four counts are at least 10.

sections.heading: Sample means and the CLT
sections.body: μ_x̄ = μ and σ_x̄ = σ/√n (10% condition). If the population is Normal, x̄ is Normal for any n. Central Limit Theorem: for any population shape, the sampling distribution of x̄ becomes approximately Normal as n grows; n ≥ 30 is a common guideline. For small samples from a skewed population, the sampling distribution of x̄ remains skewed (less so than the population). For differences of independent sample means: μ = μ₁ − μ₂ and σ = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂).

sections.heading: Using sampling distributions
sections.body: To find the probability of a sample result, check conditions, state the sampling distribution (shape, mean, SD), standardize, and compute. A very small probability for an observed statistic, under an assumed parameter value, is evidence against that assumption: this is the logic of significance tests in Units 6–9.

sections.heading: Worked example: sampling distribution of a proportion
sections.body: Suppose 40% of a city's voters support a ballot measure. For random samples of 200 voters, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion p̂ has mean 0.40 and standard deviation √(0.40 × 0.60/200) ≈ 0.0346. Since np = 80 and n(1 − p) = 120 are both at least 10, the distribution is approximately Normal. The probability that a sample shows 45% or more support is P(Z ≥ (0.45 − 0.40)/0.0346) = P(Z ≥ 1.44) ≈ 0.075.

sections.heading: Worked example: the Central Limit Theorem
sections.body: Household incomes in a town are strongly right-skewed with mean $60,000 and standard deviation $30,000. For random samples of 100 households, the sample mean x̄ has mean $60,000 and standard deviation 30,000/√100 = $3,000. Because n is large, the Central Limit Theorem says the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately Normal even though the population is skewed. The probability that x̄ exceeds $65,000 is P(Z ≥ 1.67) ≈ 0.048.

sections.heading: Bias and variability
sections.body: An unbiased estimator has a sampling distribution centered on the true parameter. Larger samples reduce variability: quadrupling the sample size halves the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. The 10% condition (n ≤ 10% of the population) ensures that observations are approximately independent when sampling without replacement.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse the population distribution, the distribution of one sample, and the sampling distribution, and they forget to check the Normal and 10% conditions.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know parameter, statistic, sampling distribution, unbiased estimator, standard deviation of a statistic, Central Limit Theorem, and the 10% and large counts conditions.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Sampling distribution questions ask you to describe the shape, center, and spread of the sampling distribution, justify Normality with the large counts condition or the Central Limit Theorem, and calculate a probability. A simulation dotplot may be provided; use it to judge whether an observed result is unusual.

sections.heading: Final tip
sections.body: Draw and label the sampling distribution before calculating any probability. Mark the mean and the value of interest, shade the region you need, and write the z-score calculation with the correct standard deviation for the statistic, not the population standard deviation.

keyTakeaways: Large Counts: np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10.
CLT: x̄ approximately Normal for large n regardless of population shape.
Larger n → less variability; doesn't fix bias.
10% condition justifies the SD formula when sampling without replacement.
commonMistakes: Saying the CLT makes the population (or the sample) Normal.
Using σ instead of σ/√n for a sample mean.
Forgetting to check Large Counts before using Normal for p̂.
Confusing the distribution of a sample with the sampling distribution.
examTips: Name the sampling distribution explicitly with shape, mean, and SD before calculating.
Justify Normal shape with the specific condition and numbers.
MCQs often test what happens to the SD when n changes.
Bias questions describe an estimator's simulated sampling distribution; compare its center to the parameter.
guide.cramSheet:
**Parameter:** p, μ, σ · **Statistic:** p̂, x̄, s

**p̂:** μ = p · σ = √(p(1 − p)/n) · Normal if np, n(1 − p) ≥ 10

**x̄:** μ = μ · σ = σ/√n · Normal if pop Normal or n ≥ 30 (CLT)

**Differences:** subtract means · add variances

**10%:** n ≤ 0.1N

**Bias:** center ≠ parameter · **Variability:** ↓ with larger n (×4 n → ½ SD)

vocab.definition: A number that describes a population.
A number that describes a sample.
The distribution of values of a statistic across all possible samples of the same size.
A statistic whose sampling distribution has a mean equal to the parameter it estimates.
The spread of its sampling distribution, which decreases as sample size increases.
For large n, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately Normal regardless of the population's shape.
np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10, so the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately Normal.
When sampling without replacement, n ≤ 10% of the population, so the SD formula is approximately correct.
A single statistic used to estimate a parameter.
A statistic whose sampling distribution is not centered at the parameter.

choices.text: It cannot be determined because the population is skewed.

practice.explanation: n = 36 ≥ 30, so by the CLT x̄ is approximately Normal with SD 15/6 = 2.5. z = 2; P ≈ 0.023.

II, because it has the least variability
III, because it is unbiased and has low variability
All are equally good

practice.explanation: III is centered at 50 with small spread; II is biased; I is unbiased but highly variable.

practice.prompt: A city council member claims that 40% of the city's voters support a new transit tax. A polling firm will take a random sample of 150 voters from the city's 220,000 registered voters.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Assuming the claim is true, describe the sampling distribution of p̂, the sample proportion who support the tax (shape, center, variability), and justify the shape.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Justify the formula you used for the standard deviation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Assuming the claim is true, find the probability that 50% or more of the sample supports the tax.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The poll finds that 75 of the 150 voters (50%) support the tax. Does this give convincing evidence that the council member's claim is too low? Explain using your answer to (c).

rubric.description: 150 is less than 10% of 220,000 voters, so sampling without replacement is approximately independent.
Yes; if the true proportion were 0.40, a sample proportion of 0.50 or higher would occur only about 0.6% of the time, so the result is convincing evidence that more than 40% support the tax.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) The sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately Normal because np = 150(0.40) = 60 and n(1 − p) = 150(0.60) = 90 are both at least 10. Its mean is p = 0.40, and its standard deviation is √(0.40 × 0.60/150) = 0.040.

(b) The sample of 150 is less than 10% of the 220,000 registered voters, so even though sampling is without replacement, the observations are approximately independent and the formula is valid.

(c) z = (0.50 − 0.40)/0.040 = 2.5. P(p̂ ≥ 0.50) = P(Z ≥ 2.5) ≈ 0.0062.

(d) Yes. If 40% of voters truly supported the tax, a random sample of 150 would give 50% or more support only about 0.62% of the time. Because this outcome is so unlikely under the claim, the poll provides convincing evidence that the true proportion of supporters is greater than 40%.
